text: Top up repair and construction materials
Keep less food in reserve, recycle and make tools more; uses the same coordinator and costs the same.
By the furnace or at the apprentice table

The first furnace is ready to fire up. The craftspeople want to stock materials for the next round of projects, while the teacher wants to keep the apprentices in class. Production and teaching compete for the same adults.
Stock materials for production first
Delegate five industrial jobs, prioritizing larger buffers of ore, coal, iron, and parts; use the remaining capacity for teaching. Material and shift costs still apply.
Teach the next group of apprentices first
Assign teachers first, and maintain only a smaller repair buffer for industry; research will progress faster, but construction materials will accumulate more slowly.
Beyond empty beds, what else should we leave?
New families brought by the convoy need tools, medicine, and classrooms. Beds are ready, but the same tools are also needed for public works.
Pause admissions and fund public services
Stop new groups from setting out, while keeping families already on the way and their beds. Reserve tools and medicine for current residents. Resume on the migration page later.
Continue admissions with support
Continue existing admission checks and pay actual travel costs; supporting the current population remains the priority, so projects may wait for materials.
Urban industry or keep farming
Workshops want to concentrate skilled workers, while farms and medical teams need to retain staff. The choice changes actual jobs in the first district, not the number of residents.
Farming and public services
Keep farms and medical staff; reduce toolmaking jobs.
Focus on recycling and toolmaking
Raise recycling, toolmaking, and material stock targets, using up other available work slots.
What comes next for treatment?
Medical staff want clinical teaching aids, while the craft guild wants to keep tools on hand first. This is a choice between ongoing expenditure and medicine production capacity.
Clinical medicine production
Use tools and knowledge for actual clinical medicine production; provide enough trained medical staff for this district's population.
Use tools and knowledge for actual clinical medicine production; requires two trained medical staff.
Maintain basic medicine production
Keep teaching aids and tools; maintain the existing recipe and output.
Who will replace the retiring teachers?
The school wants to keep enrolling students based on retirement forecasts, while operators want to keep training funds in reserve.
Delegate early recruitment
The institution enrolls students to fill actual shortages, with ongoing costs for teaching aids and food.
Open classes manually as needed
Do not automatically take on new courses; resume them manually when retirements leave vacancies.
The cost of wind, water, and fuel
Wind uses less fuel but has lulls; waterwheels are steadier, while biomass uses wood meant for civilian use.
10 power and tool maintenance per period.
6 or 12 power per period; lulls may disrupt production.
16 power per period, consumes 1.2 wood continuously, and requires tool maintenance.
Take new orders or train new workers first
Every city agreed that maintenance must be paid first, leaving too little budget to complete every task.
Training first
After maintenance, reserve the budget for courses first; shipments may be delayed.
Supplies first
After maintenance, fulfill shipping orders first; training must wait for spare budget.
Rotate each period
Switch priorities according to the existing rotation rules, without increasing the public budget.
Standardized production or local repair
Local workshops need reliable supplies of common tools; partner enterprises need more standardized products and iron shipped between cities.
Use the actual scrap and wood recipe, with lower commitments for external supply.
Use more iron and maintenance resources for production; if iron runs short, automatically switch back to repair and construction.
Let each city set its own production
Stop the institution from arranging new production; continue paying for supplies already contracted, and let each city keep its existing processes.
Who should the new community produce for?
Cooperative jobs for resettled families are already in place. Should that same work time go to farming or toolmaking?
Farming cooperative
Farming cooperative jobs produce food to support the local population.
Toolmaking cooperative
The same cooperative residents use actual materials to make tools.
Who should take responsibility for cross-district commitments?
The central institution wants authority that makes coordination easier; local representatives want to keep their own decision-making power. Both arrangements require ongoing payments.
